# Part VI. Negotiating Joint Decisions {.unnumbered}

A supplier wants a higher price, while the buyer insists on a lower one. If the conversation stays with that single number, every gain appears to be the other side's loss. Delivery timing, payment terms, volume, and reliability may offer useful trades—but only if the parties discover which differences matter.

This part follows a supplier relationship and an employment package across four chapters. We begin with preparation: what each side can do without an agreement, what an acceptable agreement must provide, and what remains uncertain. The discussion then turns to offers and concessions, followed by the differences that can make a package better for both sides.

Finally, we ask what happens after agreement. A promise needs clear terms, a way to check performance, and a response to foreseeable disagreement. Reaching a deal is useful only when the deal is worth making and can be carried out.

![A reading route through Part VI. The arrows show the progression of questions in this part.](../figures/master-loop-part-6.svg){fig-alt="Three reading questions: What are the alternatives? Where is value claimed or created? How will the agreement work?"}

## Questions to carry forward

- What can each side do if we do not agree?
- Which differences could support a useful trade?
- How will we know whether the agreement is working?

The final part carries this concern with implementation into everyday behavior, the design of choices, and the way organizations make and review decisions.
